scalesUsed.notes: G - A - B - C - D - E - F# - G
scalesUsed.application: All chords and melodies derive from the G major scale
Vocal melody and instrumental fills use this simplified scale

keyAndScale.modalCharacter: Bright, uplifting major tonality with a folk/country feel created by the open chord voicings
keyAndScale.relativeMinor: E minor is the relative minor of G major

mainProgression.description: The universally beloved four-chord progression used in the verse. One of the most common progressions in popular music, here given a folk/country character through strumming style.

sectionProgressions.description: The verse cycles through four open chords in a flowing strumming pattern, each chord lasting one full bar
The chorus simplifies to three chords, dropping the Em for a brighter, more anthemic feel during the sing-along 'Rock me mama' sections

harmonicFunction: G (I) - Tonic chord providing the bright, home-key foundation
D (V) - Dominant chord creating movement and energy, resolving naturally back to G
Em (vi) - Relative minor chord adding emotional depth and color in the verse
C (IV) - Subdominant chord providing warmth and the sense of journey and longing

techniques.name: Folk Strumming Pattern
techniques.description: A flowing down-up strumming pattern in a country/folk style that gives Wagon Wheel its driving, feel-good groove

notes: G: 3-2-0-0-3-3 (full open G with fingers on 3rd fret low E and both high strings)
D: X-X-0-2-3-2 (open D major chord)
Em: 0-2-2-0-0-0 (open E minor chord)
C: X-3-2-0-1-0 (open C major chord)
Each chord gets one full bar (4 beats) in the verse progression
sequence: Learn all four open chord shapes: G, D, Em, C
Practice the basic strumming pattern: Down - Down-Up - Up-Down-Up
Apply the pattern to each chord individually
Connect the verse progression: G - D - Em - C with the strumming pattern
tips: Keep your strumming hand moving in a steady down-up motion even during rests
The transition from G to D is the most common - practice it until automatic
Let the open strings ring out for a full, warm sound
This is a campfire song - keep it relaxed and singable
details.progression: G - D - Em - C (verse) | G - D - C (chorus)

techniques.name: Chord Transition Technique
techniques.description: Smooth transitions between the four open chords using common fingers as pivot points, essential for maintaining the flowing feel of the song

notes: G to D: Lift fingers from G shape, place ring finger on 3rd fret B string first, then middle and index
D to Em: Simply lift the D shape and place index and middle fingers on 2nd fret A and D strings
Em to C: Keep the middle finger in placthe note at the correct fret position as a pivot, add ring and index
C to G: The ring finger moves from 3rd fret A string to 3rd fret low E string
sequence: Practice G to D transition 20 times slowly, then with strumming
Practice D to Em transition 20 times - this is the easiest change
Practice Em to C using the common finger pivot
Practice C to G to complete the cycle, then loop all four
tips: Look for common fingers between chords to use as anchors
Lift and place all fingers simultaneously rather than one at a time
Practice chord changes without strumming first, just switching shapes
Speed will come naturally with repetition - focus on accuracy first

sections.name: Intro
sections.description: Brief instrumental intro establishing the key and tempo with the verse chord progression
notes: The intro uses the verse progression to establish the groove
Start with a confident G chord strum
Original recording features fiddle - guitar provides the rhythmic foundation
Set the tempo at a brisk 152 BPM from the start

sections.name: Verse
sections.description: The storytelling verses about traveling down south, using the four-chord progression with a steady folk strum
notes: Each chord gets one full bar with the folk strumming pattern
The progression repeats for each pair of lyric lines
Keep the dynamics moderate for the verse - save energy for the chorus
Focus on steady, even strumming throughout

sections.name: Chorus
sections.description: The anthemic the signature chorus using the simplified three-chord pattern for maximum sing-along energy
notes: Increase strumming intensity for the chorus
The Em drops out, making the chorus brighter and more uplifting
This is the big sing-along moment - strum with confidence
The C chord gets extra time in the chorus pattern

sections.name: Outro
sections.description: Final chorus repetitions building to the joyful ending, often with audience participation in live settings
notes: Repeat the chorus progression with maximum energy
Build to a big final G chord to end the song
Let the final G chord ring out fully
This is a crowd-pleasing singalong moment in live performance

guitar.recommended: Martin D-28 or any dreadnought acoustic guitar
guitar.pickup: Acoustic guitar - no pickup needed. For amplified performance, use an acoustic pickup or microphone.

amp.recommended: Acoustic guitar amp or PA system
alternatives: No amplification needed for campfire/small group playing

effects.reverb: Light natural reverb for room ambiance
effects.other: No effects needed. This is a pure acoustic strumming song. A good quality pick (medium gauge) is recommended.

beginner.focus: Learn the four open chords and basic strumming
steps: Learn G, D, Em, and C open chord shapes individually
Practice transitioning between each pair of chords
Learn a basic down-strum pattern at slow tempo
Play through the verse progression: G - D - Em - C

intermediate.focus: Master the strumming pattern and play the full song
steps: Learn the full folk strumming pattern: Down - Down-Up - Up-Down-Up
Apply the strumming pattern to both verse and chorus progressions
Build up to 152 BPM with a metronome
Play through the entire song from intro to outro without stopping

advanced.focus: Sing while playing and add embellishments
steps: Practice singing the melody while strumming the chords
Add hammer-ons and pull-offs to embellish chord changes
Experiment with fingerpicking patterns for a quieter version
Learn to lead a group sing-along with this song

commonMistakes: Rushing the tempo - keep it steady at 152 BPM, not faster
Struggling with the G to D transition - this needs the most practice
Strumming too hard on the verse - save dynamics for the chorus
Forgetting the chorus drops the Em chord - keep verse and chorus patterns distinct
practiceRoutine: Warm up with G, D, Em, C chord changes for 3 minutes
Practice the strumming pattern on a single chord for 2 minutes
Play through the verse progression (G-D-Em-C) 4 times with strumming
Play through the chorus progression (G-D-C) 4 times with increased energy
Run through the entire song structure from start to finish
focusAreas: Smooth chord transitions, especially G to D
Dynamic contrast between verse and chorus
metronomeWork: Start at 100 BPM with the four-chord progression
Increase by 10 BPM each session until reaching 152 BPM
Practice the chord changes at tempo without strumming pattern first
Add the full strumming pattern once chord changes are solid at tempo
